TinyFish, a web infrastructure […] The post TinyFish Makes Search Free: What It Really Costs an AI Agent to Read the Web appeared first on MarkTechPost . ]]> An AI agent that reads the web pays 2 kinds of cost. The first is the retrieval charge: what a search or fetch API bills per request. The second is model processing: content passed from retrieved pages into an AI model consumes tokens, while reasoning and generated responses add further costs. TinyFish , a web infrastructure company for AI agents, argues that teams budget for the model and underestimate how much retrieved content drives it. This article walks through the token math, the context-window impact, and what the Artificial Analysis Search API leaderboard does and does not show. TL;DR What it runs on: TinyFish uses a web-native AI model designed for search, retrieval, and interaction with live websites. The model runs on TinyFish-managed infrastructure, while its cloud browser fleet renders pages and handles website interactions. No local GPU is needed. Access is via REST, Python and TypeScript SDKs, CLI or MCP. Performance: On the Sep 28, 2026 Artificial Analysis snapshot, TinyFish Search (web) scores 71 at $9.30 per 1,000 benchmark tasks, with 59.0 seconds per task (model plus search time). Best: $0 retrieval charge within rate limits (Search: 30 requests/min, 500/hour; Fetch: 150 URLs/min, 1,000/day), and the lowest total cost among the 12 configurations displayed on the leaderboard. Trade-offs: The second longest time per task among displayed configurations, and an Agent product whose built-in model cannot be swapped. Scores: Highest displayed is Perplexity Search (medium) at 80. Lowest displayed is TinyFish Search (web) at 71. The no-search baseline is 33. Retrieval charges vs model processing costs Search and fetch APIs usually bill per request or per page. Whatever they return then enters the model’s context and is billed as input tokens. Reasoning and output tokens come on top. Enterprises now route each task to the cheapest capable model, a trend underlined when Stripe agreed to acquire OpenRouter , a gateway spanning 400+ models from 80+ providers. Routing lowers the price per token. It does not change how many tokens a retrieved page contains. Free Search and Fetch remove TinyFish’s retrieval charge within its limits. The downstream model still incurs inference costs. That is why the size of each returned page matters. How big is one page in tokens? TinyFish ran a fetch quality evaluation on June 2, 2026, across 45 URLs and 5 providers on default settings. For one Daily Mail article with a body of roughly 4,300 characters, the providers returned: Provider Characters returned Est. tokens* Input cost at $1 / 1M tokens* TinyFish Fetch 4,737 ~1,184 ~$0.00118 Exa Contents 65,793 ~16,448 ~$0.01645 Firecrawl Scrape 171,095 ~42,774 ~$0.04277 Tavily Extract 46,433 ~11,608 ~$0.01161 Parallel Extract 600 (excerpt, not the article) ~150 ~$0.00015 *Marktechpost calculation: ~4 characters per token and an illustrative input price of $1 per 1M tokens. Input processing only; excludes retrieval charges, reasoning and output. Real counts vary by tokenizer. Character counts from TinyFish’s evaluation. In this example, Firecrawl returned approximately 36 times as many characters as TinyFish.  Parallel also returned only an excerpt rather than the complete article, so its smaller output is not directly comparable to the full-page extractions. While this illustrates how extraction output size can affect token consumption, the difference comes from a single webpage and should not be generalized across all websites. Those percentages are not used for this individual page comparison because outputs above 30,000 characters were truncated before judging. Context limits and repeated calls Assume every extracted character goes into the same context, with no filtering, truncation or summarization. A page containing approximately 42,774 tokens would consume about one-third of a 128K-token context window. Three such pages would require approximately 128,322 tokens, leaving little or no room for system instructions, conversation history, or the agent’s response. Agent loops also resend context. Artificial Analysis notes that each turn resends the full conversation, with earlier input billed at the model’s cached-input price. Caching lowers the cost of rereading a noisy page. It does not remove it, and the page still occupies the window. In that TinyFish internal evaluation, a result counted as covered only with at least 1,000 characters and a judged signal ratio above 30%. Coverage was TinyFish 93%, Tavily 80%, Exa 73%, Firecrawl 62% and Parallel 58%. Among usable results only, median signal was 90.5% for TinyFish and 89.7% for Exa. TinyFish ran the test on itself, the sample is 45 URLs, and news pages drove most of the gap. Why TinyFish makes retrieval free TinyFish frames search as one operation inside execution, like DNS or storage for ordinary software. An agent booking, comparing or filling out a form should care whether the job got done, not which search system found the page.  TinyFish attributes its free retrieval pricing to three aspects of its infrastructure: Shared infrastructure: TinyFish built its browser fleet, stealth systems, session hydration and elastic scaling before Search was a product. TinyFish says this changes the marginal economics of search. It does not make the infrastructure free to run. Specialized models: TinyFish says its web-native AI model is designed for search, fetch, and live-site interaction. Its development draws on agent operational trajectories and large volumes of search activity, helping reduce reliance on general-purpose models for intermediate web tasks. No giant index: TinyFish says it would rather learn how work gets done than become an indexing company. TinyFish charges separately for Agent and Browser usage, while Search and Fetch remain free within their published limits. Per the pricing page , Search is free at 30 requests per minute and 500 per hour. Fetch is free at 150 URLs per minute and 1,000 per day. Both keep working at a $0 Wallet balance. Agent costs $0.016 per step with 2 concurrent runs, and Browser costs $0.002 per minute with 5 sessions. New accounts get $8 in Wallet funds. What the benchmark shows, and what it does not Artificial Analysis holds the answer model fixed (GPT-5.6 Luna, medium) and changes only the search provider. Model cost covers input, cached, reasoning and output tokens. Differences between providers reflect returned payloads, how many searches the model runs and how much it reasons. On the Sep 28, 2026 snapshot, model cost ranges from $8.04 to $21.65 per 1,000 tasks across the 12 displayed configurations. These come from 26 products across 13 providers. TinyFish posts $0 for search plus $9.30 for the model, the lowest displayed total. The trade-offs: TinyFish recorded a Search Index score of 71, the lowest among the displayed configurations, and a DeepSearchQA F1 of 67. API pricing is $0.15/$0.60 per 1M tokens, with weights due October 23 The post MiniMax Just Launched M3.1 Flash: 428B MoE Agentic Model at $0.15/M Input appeared first on MarkTechPost . ]]> MiniMax has just released MiniMax M3.1 Flash on its API, priced at $0.15 per 1M input tokens . MiniMax also confirmed that Space Bunny was an earlier M3.1 Flash build. That stealth model processed over 200T tokens. For developers, the message is near-frontier agentic scores at Flash-tier cost. Model weights are due in late October, 2026. TL;DR Size: 428B total parameters, about 23B active (MoE); 1,000,000-token context Runs on: MiniMax API, M Plan and MiniMax Code today. Self-hosting hardware not disclosed; weights arrive Oct 23 Performance: Near-frontier on agentic office work, mid-pack on hard coding, all MiniMax-reported Best: Automation-Bench v1.0.6 at 62.2, the top score in MiniMax’s table Worst: Terminal Bench 4.0 at 38.1, versus 51.8 for Opus 5 What is MiniMax M3.1 Flash? MiniMax M3.1 Flash is a multimodal mixture-of-experts model from MiniMax. It targets coding, agentic office work and visual reasoning. MiniMax’s product page lists 428B total parameters and about 23B active. It also mentions sparse attention and a native visual encoder. The model accepts text, image and video input and returns text. The context window is 1,000,000 tokens. Those parameter totals match MiniMax M3 , which ships at ~428B total and ~23B active. MiniMax has not published a technical report on what changed in the Flash variant. How does reasoning work in M3.1 Flash? Reasoning is always on and cannot be disabled. Developers choose from 5 effort levels: Low, Medium, High, Xhigh and Max. MiniMax recommends Max as the default. Migration matters here. Requests sending thinking.type=disabled or effort=none return an error. Reasoning arrives in a separate reasoning_content field, which may be absent. Integrations that parse inline <think> tags from M3 need updating. How does M3.1 Flash perform on benchmarks? All scores below are MiniMax-reported. No independent replication exists yet. On the CoWork set, M3.1 Flash leads Automation-Bench v1.0.6 at 62.2 . Opus 5 scores 50.3 and GPT-5.6 Sol 45.8. It ties Opus 5 on BankerToolBench at 76.2. It also tops LOCA-Bench 256K at 60.3. Agents’ Last Exam lands at 29.6. Coding results are mixed. DeepSWE v1.1 scores 73.7, just above GPT-5.6 Sol at 73.0. DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017 scores higher at 77.0. Terminal Bench 4.0 is the weakest result at 38.1. SWE Refactor Bench sits at 23.0, versus 31.0 for Opus 5. On vision, BabyVision with tools reaches 91.0 and CharXiv RQ reaches 82.5. HLE without tools scores 43.4. Spot checks hold up. The Kimi K3 model card reports DeepSWE 67.5 and BabyVision 85.7, matching MiniMax’s table. One inconsistency: MiniMax’s cost chart plots Automation-Bench max effort at 62.8, while its table says 62.2. What does M3.1 Flash cost per task? MiniMax frames value as cost per task, not per token. On its Automation-Bench chart, all 5 effort levels sit below $0.05 per task. Scores range from 52.8 at low effort to 62.8 at max. A full 152-task Agents’ Last Exam run cost about $111 at 29.6. On DeepSWE, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash-1017 plots both higher and cheaper at max effort. How do you deploy MiniMax M3.1 Flash? The model is live on platform.minimax.io as MiniMax-M3.1-Flash . MiniMax supports Anthropic-compatible and OpenAI-compatible access, including Chat Completions and Responses. It is also available through M Plan and the MiniMax Code desktop app . Pricing is a flat $0.15 input and $0.60 output per 1M tokens. Cache reads cost $0.015 per 1M. There is no long-context surcharge. MiniMax M3 costs $0.30/$1.20 up to 512K input and doubles above that. Per token, Flash is half of M3’s standard rate. MiniMax claims 1/3 the cost of M3 but has not detailed the calculation. On speed, MiniMax’s product page lists about 150 tokens per second. The announcement claims 3x the speed of M3. Weights arrive October 23; the license is not yet disclosed. For scale, M3’s MXFP8 build is about 440 GB . How does M3.1 Flash compare with DeepSeek, Kimi and GLM? Feature MiniMax M3.1 Flash DeepSeek V4.1 Flash Kimi K3 GLM-5.3 Total / active params 428B / ~23B ( MiniMax ) 552B / 8B prefill, 16B decode ( NVIDIA card ) 2.8T / 104B ( HF ) ~744B / ~40B, shared GLM-5 base Context 1M 1M ( DeepSeek docs ) 1,048,576 1,048,576 ( Cloudflare ) Inputs Text, image, video Text, image Text, image Text Weights / license Due Oct 23; license not disclosed Open, MIT Open, Kimi K3 License Open weights API price in / out (1M) $0.15 / $0.60 flat $0.30 / $1.20 peak; half off-peak $3.00 / $15.00 $1.40 / $4.40 Self-host hardware Not disclosed Not disclosed MXFP4 weights; vLLM, SGLang Not disclosed Automation-Bench v1.0.6* 62.2 54.8 46.7 48.8 DeepSWE v1.1* 73.7 74.2 67.5 66.9 Terminal Bench 4.0* 38.1 31.2 12.6 37.9 BabyVision (w/ tools)* 91.0 89.6 85.7 Not reported *Scores from MiniMax’s comparison table . Kimi K3 DeepSWE and BabyVision match its own card. What are the limitations? Every benchmark is vendor-reported, and harness choice shifts results. Automation-Bench numbers do not transfer across sources. Kimi K3’s card reports 30.8 on a 600-task public subset, while MiniMax lists 46.7. Opus 5 leads by 13.7 points on Terminal Bench 4.0 and 14.1 on NL2Repo-Bench. Always-on reasoning also sets a token and latency floor for simple calls. Self-hosting details remain unknown until October 23. Key Takeaways 428B MoE with ~23B active and a 1M context. $0.15/$0.60 per 1M tokens, half of M3’s per-token rate. Leads Automation-Bench v1.0.6 at 62.2, MiniMax-reported. Trails Opus 5 by 13.7 points on Terminal Bench 4.0. Weights land Oct 23; reasoning cannot be disabled. Check out the announcement , product page and API docs . All credit goes to the researcher of this project. MiniMax M3.1 Flash is a multimodal mixture-of-experts model from MiniMax. It targets coding, agentic office work and visual reasoning. MiniMax’s product page lists 428B total parameters and about 23B active. It also mentions sparse attention and a native visual encoder. The model accepts text, image and video input and returns text. The context window is 1,000,000 tokens. Those parameter totals match MiniMax M3 , which ships at ~428B total and ~23B active. MiniMax has not published a technical report on what changed in the Flash variant. How does reasoning work in M3.1 Flash? Reasoning is always on and cannot be disabled. Developers choose from 5 effort levels: Low, Medium, High, Xhigh and Max. MiniMax recommends Max as the default. Migration matters here. Requests sending thinking.type=disabled or effort=none return an error. Reasoning arrives in a separate reasoning_content field, which may be absent. Integrations that parse inline <think> tags from M3 need updating. How does M3.1 Flash perform on benchmarks? All scores below are MiniMax-reported. No independent replication exists yet. On the CoWork set, M3.1 Flash leads Automation-Bench v1.0.6 at 62.2 . Opus 5 scores 50.3 and GPT-5.6 Sol 45.8. It ties Opus 5 on BankerToolBench at 76.2. It also tops LOCA-Bench 256K at 60.3. Terminal Bench 4.0 is the weakest result at 38.1. SWE Refactor Bench sits at 23.0, versus 31.0 for Opus 5. On vision, BabyVision with tools reaches 91.0 and CharXiv RQ reaches 82.5. HLE without tools scores 43.4. Spot checks hold up. The Kimi K3 model card reports DeepSWE 67.5 and BabyVision 85.7, matching MiniMax’s table. One inconsistency: MiniMax’s cost chart plots Automation-Bench max effort at 62.8, while its table says 62.2. What does M3.1 Flash cost per task? MiniMax frames value as cost per task, not per token. On its Automation-Bench chart, all 5 effort levels sit below $0.05 per task. Scores range from 52.8 at low effort to 62.8 at max. A full 152-task Agents’ Last Exam run cost about $111 at 29.6. On DeepSWE, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash-1017 plots both higher and cheaper at max effort. How do you deploy MiniMax M3.1 Flash? The model is live on platform.minimax.io as MiniMax-M3.1-Flash . MiniMax supports Anthropic-compatible and OpenAI-compatible access, including Chat Completions and Responses. It is also available through M Plan and the MiniMax Code desktop app . Pricing is a flat $0.15 input and $0.60 output per 1M tokens. Cache reads cost $0.015 per 1M. There is no long-context surcharge. MiniMax M3 costs $0.30/$1.20 up to 512K input and doubles above that. Per token, Flash is half of M3’s standard rate. MiniMax claims 1/3 the cost of M3 but has not detailed the calculation. On speed, MiniMax’s product page lists about 150 tokens per second. The announcement claims 3x the speed of M3. Weights arrive October 23; the license is not yet disclosed. For scale, M3’s MXFP8 build is about 440 GB . The post Inception Releases Mercury 3 Diffusion LLM at 1,068 Tokens per Second appeared first on MarkTechPost . ]]> Inception has released Mercury 3 , the newest version of its diffusion language model. Mercury 3 is a diffusion LLM from Inception that writes answers in parallel, not token by token. Inception reports 1,068 tokens per second on NVIDIA GPUs and a 1M-token context window. On Inception’s own benchmark table, it leads GPT-6 Luna and Claude Haiku 5.5 on 8 of 12 tests. For developers building agents, voice bots and search tools, this is a speed-first model with competitive scores. TL;DR Size: Parameters not disclosed. Inception says it is more than 40x larger than Mercury 1. Context is 1M tokens. Runs on: Inception-served NVIDIA GPUs (exact GPU not disclosed). API only, no open weights or quantized builds. Performance: Leads 8 of 12 benchmarks vs GPT-6 Luna and Haiku 5.5 (self-reported, medium settings). Best: SWE-Bench Atlas 51.08, about 18 points ahead of both rivals. Worst: DeepSWE v1 46.31, 5.31 points behind Haiku 5.5 (51.62). What is Mercury 3? Mercury 3 is Inception’s fourth Mercury release, after Mercury 1, Mercury 2 and Mercury 2.5. Mercury 1 launched in 2025. Mercury 2.5 added tunable reasoning and a 260K context window, per Inception’s launch announcement . 1/4 Today, we’re releasing Mercury 3. Mercury 3 is by far our most powerful model and the most intelligent diffusion LLM ever released. It outperforms GPT-6 Luna and Haiku 5.5 on quality while running at 1000+ tok/sec. pic.twitter.com/TYevDl43Lm — Stefano Ermon (@StefanoErmon) October 19, 2026 How does a diffusion LLM work? Autoregressive models write one token after another. Each new token waits for the previous one. A diffusion LLM starts from a rough draft of the full answer. It then refines every position over a few passes in parallel. Fewer sequential steps means faster output on the same GPUs. The open question was whether this approach holds up as models grow larger. Does diffusion scale? Here Inception’s answer is yes. Mercury 3 has more than 40x the total parameters of Mercury 1 (mini). Average quality across standard benchmarks rose about 3x between those 2 models. Speed stayed above 1,000 tokens per second. Inception team plots this as a quality vs size curve across 5 Mercury generations. How does Mercury 3 perform on benchmarks? All scores below come from Inception’s table . Every model ran at medium settings. Mercury 3 posts its largest gains on instruction following and agentic coding. IFBench reaches 76.84, 15 points above GPT-6 Luna. SWE-Bench Atlas reaches 51.08, against 33.33 for Luna and 32.26 for Haiku 5.5. GPQA Diamond lands at 89.23. The losses matter too. Haiku 5.5 wins DeepSWE v1 (51.62 vs 46.31) and MRCR v2 (78.40 vs 75.50). GPT-6 Luna edges ahead on AA-Omniscience-Public (46.94 vs 46.44) and AA-LCR v1.1 (78.30 vs 77.67). Long-context retrieval and longer coding tasks remain the weak spots. Specs and prices: each vendor’s own docs. What do early users report? Inception quotes 4 early-access partners. These are customer statements, not independent evals. TinyFish ran 50 live Mind2Web web-navigation tasks. Mercury 3 completed 50% of them. Inception says that beat GPT-6.1-Sol but gives no Sol number. Octen AI reports 0.9 seconds median generation and 2.2 seconds end to end for smart-glasses search. RevisionDojo says hints and marked answers return in about a second. Lorikeet says Mercury 3 beat other models on latency and evals for support agents. How can developers use Mercury 3? Mercury 3 is live on the Inception API Platform , OpenRouter , Baseten and Vercel. The API is OpenAI compatible. The docs use the model string mercury-3 and a reasoning_effort parameter. List pricing is $0.20 per 1M input and $0.70 per 1M output tokens. At launch it is 50% off: $0.10 and $0.35. Cached input is 90% off. New accounts get 100M free tokens. Enterprise plans add dedicated capacity, autoscaling and configurable data retention. Inception also ships 2 siblings : Mercury Voice targets time to first answer token in voice agents. Mercury Decide is a classification model. The post Inception Releases Mercury 3 Diffusion LLM at 1,068 Tokens per Second appeared first on MarkTechPost . ]]> Inception has released Mercury 3 , the newest version of its diffusion language model. Mercury 3 is a diffusion LLM from Inception that writes answers in parallel, not token by token. Inception reports 1,068 tokens per second on NVIDIA GPUs and a 1M-token context window. On Inception’s own benchmark table, it leads GPT-6 Luna and Claude Haiku 5.5 on 8 of 12 tests. For developers building agents, voice bots and search tools, this is a speed-first model with competitive scores. TL;DR Size: Parameters not disclosed. Inception says it is more than 40x larger than Mercury 1. Context is 1M tokens. Runs on: Inception-served NVIDIA GPUs (exact GPU not disclosed). API only, no open weights or quantized builds. Performance: Leads 8 of 12 benchmarks vs GPT-6 Luna and Haiku 5.5 (self-reported, medium settings). Best: SWE-Bench Atlas 51.08, about 18 points ahead of both rivals. Worst: DeepSWE v1 46.31, 5.31 points behind Haiku 5.5 (51.62). What is Mercury 3? Mercury 3 is Inception’s fourth Mercury release, after Mercury 1, Mercury 2 and Mercury 2.5. Mercury 1 launched in 2025. Mercury 2.5 added tunable reasoning and a 260K context window, per Inception’s launch announcement . 1/4 Today, we’re releasing Mercury 3. Mercury 3 is by far our most powerful model and the most intelligent diffusion LLM ever released. It outperforms GPT-6 Luna and Haiku 5.5 on quality while running at 1000+ tok/sec. pic.twitter.com/TYevDl43Lm — Stefano Ermon (@StefanoErmon) October 19, 2026 How does a diffusion LLM work? Autoregressive models write one token after another. Each new token waits for the previous one. A diffusion LLM starts from a rough draft of the full answer. It then refines every position over a few passes in parallel. Fewer sequential steps means faster output on the same GPUs. The open question was whether this approach holds up as models grow larger. Does diffusion scale? Here Inception’s answer is yes. Mercury 3 has more than 40x the total parameters of Mercury 1 (mini). Average quality across standard benchmarks rose about 3x between those 2 models. Speed stayed above 1,000 tokens per second. Inception team plots this as a quality vs size curve across 5 Mercury generations. How does Mercury 3 perform on benchmarks? All scores below come from Inception’s table . Every model ran at medium settings. Mercury 3 posts its largest gains on instruction following and agentic coding. IFBench reaches 76.84, 15 points above GPT-6 Luna. SWE-Bench Atlas reaches 51.08, against 33.33 for Luna and 32.26 for Haiku 5.5. GPQA Diamond lands at 89.23. The losses matter too. Haiku 5.5 wins DeepSWE v1 (51.62 vs 46.31) and MRCR v2 (78.40 vs 75.50). GPT-6 Luna edges ahead on AA-Omniscience-Public (46.94 vs 46.44) and AA-LCR v1.1 (78.30 vs 77.67). Long-context retrieval and longer coding tasks remain the weak spots. The post Exa 3.0 Search API Tops Perplexity, Brave and Parallel on 8 Benchmarks appeared first on MarkTechPost . ]]> Exa has released Exa 3.0 , an upgrade to its web search API for AI agents. The Exa 3.0 search API ships a larger embedding model and a cheaper search type, Exa Lite. Dynamic Highlights is now generally available. Exa claims that it leads Perplexity, Brave and Parallel on 8 benchmarks. Those benchmarks were run by Exa, so you can treat them as self-reported. For developers, the practical change is cost: Lite costs $4 per 1,000 requests . TL;DR Size: Exa tracks over 2 trillion URLs and serves 100 billion pages. Embedding model size: Not disclosed. Runs on: Hosted API only. Exa lists configurable search latency of 450ms to 1s . No self-hosted option. Performance: Exa 3.0 Auto ranks first on all 8 Exa-run benchmarks against Perplexity, Brave and Parallel. Best: 91.8% on BrowseComp, plus the widest lead on ATLAS (42.0% vs 37.2% for Perplexity). Worst: 42.0% on ATLAS is its lowest percentage score. Its BrowseComp lead over Perplexity is only 0.3 points. What is Exa 3.0? Exa 3.0 is a search API release from Exa Labs that upgrades retrieval quality across every search type. It is available through the API. Exa runs its own crawler and an independent index. It is not a wrapper on Google or Bing results. How does Exa 3.0 improve retrieval? Exa attributes the gains to 3 changes in its retrieval stack: A larger embedding model : Exa trained it with more compute and data than any earlier model. Parameter count is not disclosed. Dynamic Highlights, now generally available : The model selects tokens across all results, not page by page. It gives more tokens to better pages and drops repeated information. Billions of new documents : New coverage includes products, local businesses, flights, events, sports and weather. According to the Exa’s post, Dynamic Highlights uses 95% fewer tokens than full page text while improving answer quality. Highlights carry no extra charge. That matters for agents, where context tokens often cost more than search calls. What is Exa Lite? Exa Lite is a new search type, set with type: "lite" on the /search endpoint, per the changelog . It runs on the same index as Exa Auto. Auto spends more compute on candidate generation, highlights and ranking. Lite supports query, result count, highlights, text, categories, domain and date filters, location and moderation. Unsupported parameters return a 400 error naming the field. Exa now recommends 3 search types: lite , auto and deep . The fast , instant and deep-reasoning types are legacy but still work. How does Exa 3.0 perform on benchmarks? Exa compared each provider’s highest-scoring single-step endpoint: Exa 3.0 Auto, Perplexity Web, Brave LLM Context and Parallel Advanced. All ran in one agentic harness. The agent was GPT-6 Luna, with up to 25 search rounds and 10 results per search. Evaluation happened in October 2026. The margins vary widely. ATLAS and WebCode show the clearest leads, at 4.8 and 5.6 points over Perplexity. BrowseComp, DSQA and WideSearch leads are each under 1.5 points over the runner-up. ATLAS is a benchmark Exa published itself on October 8, 2026. On cost, Exa plots agentic search score against cost per task. Lite scores about 79 at about $0.045 per task. Auto scores about 80.5 at about $0.065. Exa says the pair sets a new Pareto frontier among tested providers. How does Exa 3.0 compare with Perplexity, Brave and Parallel? Feature Exa 3.0 Auto Perplexity Search API Brave Search API (LLM Context) Parallel Search API (Advanced) List price per 1K requests $7 (Lite $4) $5 $5 $5 BrowseComp (accuracy) 91.8% 91.5% 83.5% 63.1% DSQA (F1) 88.2% 87.6% 78.6% 82.8% WideSearch (F1) 56.1% 54.0% 54.8% 53.7% ATLAS 42.0% 37.2% 28.2% 24.8% WebCode 75.5% 69.9% 68.0% 64.5% FinSearchComp 68.0% 63.4% 57.6% 66.0% Company FindAll (mean entities) 15.4 14.2 13.3 9.7 People FindAll (mean entities) 7.6 6.8 3.8 3.8 Embedding model size Not disclosed Not disclosed Not disclosed Not disclosed All benchmark scores come from Exa’s Exa 3.0 post and were run by Exa. No vendor has published matching results. Prices come from each vendor’s own pricing page. What data does the expanded index add? Exa states that it prioritized personal AI assistant use cases. The official technical page lists 1.27B ecommerce listings with prices and availability, and 211M+ local businesses . It also adds real-time news, sports, weather and market data, along with flights, events, transit and podcasts. The Exa Library structures this data into searchable collections. These include 320M people pages, 33M company pages and 500M research paper pages. It also lists 19M SEC filings, 10M patents and 9M court opinions. Where does Exa 3.0 fall short? Self-run evals : Exa picked the harness, endpoints and agent model. ATLAS is Exa’s own benchmark. Thin margins : Several leads are under 2 points, which may not survive other harnesses. Lite limits : Lite rejects unsupported parameters with a 400 , so some pipelines need Auto. Higher Auto list price : Auto costs $7 per 1,000 requests versus $5 for the 3 rivals. Opaque model details : Embedding model size and architecture are not disclosed. Key Takeaways Exa 3.0 leads 8 benchmarks, all run by Exa itself. Exa Lite costs $4 per 1,000 requests on the same index as Auto. Dynamic Highlights uses 95% fewer tokens than full pages, at no extra cost. Biggest leads: WebCode (+5.6) and ATLAS (+4.8) over Perplexity. Test on your own queries before switching providers. oldContent: Crunchbase News https://news.crunchbase.com/ Data-driven reporting on private markets, startups, founders, and investors Mon, 19 Oct 2026 17:14:32 +0000 en-US hourly 1 https://wordpress.org/?v=6.8.11 https://news.crunchbase.com/wp-content/uploads/cb_news_favicon-150x150.png Crunchbase News https://news.crunchbase.com/ 32 32 LatAm Startup Funding Jumps 26% In Q3 As VCs Begin ‘Rediscovering’ The Region https://news.crunchbase.com/venture/q3-2026-latam-startup-funding-jumps-ai-fintech-mexico/ Mon, 19 Oct 2026 11:00:46 +0000 https://news.crunchbase.com/?p=94241 A continued boom in late-stage and growth funding combined with a surge in seed-stage funding helped buoy venture investment in Latin America for the third quarter of 2026, Crunchbase data shows. All told, startups in Latin America raised a combined $1.3 billion across seed- and growth-stage deals in the three-month period ending Sept. 30. That was up 26% year over year but down 9% from the second quarter. For perspective, we charted out total investment, color-coded by stage, for the past 12 quarters below. Of the quarterly total, $757 million went into late-stage and growth deals, up 74% compared to the $435 million that flowed into such deals in the third quarter of 2025. However, that is down 21.3% from the $962 million in late-stage and growth rounds raised by LatAm startups in the second quarter. (Although it’s worth noting that Q2 2026 represented the most raised at that stage since the second quarter of 2022.) Mexico startups have raised $1.52 billion in venture funding during the first three quarters of 2026, per Crunchbase data. Notably, that’s about 40.7% more than the $1.08 billion Brazil’s startups raised in the same period. This is unusual as Brazil has historically been the largest recipient of venture funding in Latin America. Still, Brazil continues to attract a broad range of investors. “Over the past year, we have seen investments into Brazil from firms including Sequoia , Founders Fund , NEA , Battery and Tidemark ,” Allen Taylor , managing partner of Endeavor Catalyst , told Crunchbase News. “For several, this marked either their first investment in Latin America or their first in a long time.” Igor Piquet , Endeavor Catalyst’s vice president and head of Latin America, noted that Mexico drew more venture funding in the first half of 2026 than Brazil. But much of Mexico’s funding went to a few startups, he pointed out, while Brazil recorded many deals. “Investors are concentrating on a few Mexican winners, while Brazil retains the breadth,” Piquet said, adding that Brazil also leads in realized exits. Table of contents Outsized rounds An uptick in seed funding ‘Another rediscovery moment’ Methodology Glossary of funding terms Outsized rounds Several mega-raises took place in Latin America in the third quarter. And notably, the two largest funding deals were not for companies in Brazil or Mexico, which have historically raised the largest share of venture capital in the region. They also weren’t to fintech, which typically has the most funding recipients in the region, but rather to energy-related startups. Black Giant , the Chilean project company for EnergyX ’s Black Giant lithium project, raised $225 million in a July round at a reported $900 million valuation. And Colombia’s Erco Energía , a clean energy company that builds and operates solar power systems for homes and businesses, landed a $129 million Series C in August at a reported $600 million valuation. Mexico’s Kapital , an AI-powered financial services company, raised a $125 million Series C in September at a $1.6 billion valuation. Tru Arrow Partners led the financing, which included a senior debt funding facility provided by Fasanara Capital . And in August, Brazilian fintech Kesh Bank brought in $106.9 million in an equity and debt seed round at a $626 million valuation. Also in August, Brazil’s Decade , an AI-native wealth advisory company, landed $85 million in what Crunchbase data shows is the largest seed funding deal ever raised for a Latin American startup. Founded by Vitor Olivier , former CTO of Nubank , and Felipe Meneses , founder of Hyperplane AI , the startup is backed by Benchmark , Greenoaks , Diffusion , Norte Ventures and Atlantico . An uptick in seed funding Latin America experienced a marked surge in very early-stage funding totals in the third quarter, largely thanks to the seed rounds mentioned above. Of the $1.3 billion raised by Latin America’s startups in the third quarter, about 20.5% — or $266 million — was raised across the angel and seed stages. That’s up 128% from the $117 million raised across those stages in the second quarter of 2026, and up 62% from the $165 million in the same quarter last year. Just over 22%, or $288 million, was raised at early stages, down 18.9% from $355 million in the second quarter and 34% from $437 million in the same period last year. We expect the Q3 deal counts to rise somewhat over time; however, as seed rounds in particular are commonly reported weeks or months after they close. ‘Another rediscovery moment’ Latin America is drawing renewed interest from international venture investors, according to Endeavor’s Taylor. He said international VCs were more active in the region, particularly Brazil, during the first three quarters of 2026 than in 2024 and 2025 combined, through both new investments and follow-on funding. “I joke that investors from the U.S. ‘rediscover’ Latin America every five or six years, and I think we are approaching another rediscovery moment,” Taylor told Crunchbase News. Endeavor Catalyst recently closed its oversubscribed $320 million fifth fund. Latin America accounts for nearly 40% of its portfolio by both deals and dollars, and Fund V had made 14 investments in the region as of Sept. 22. Taylor also pointed to opportunities beyond Brazil and Mexico, including repeat founders building global businesses from Colombia and emerging companies in Venezuela and Central America. Liquidity is improving, although acquisitions and secondary transactions are providing more opportunities than public listings, Piquet said. He pointed to approximately 60 private Latin American technology companies that have each raised at least $150 million as a potential pipeline for future IPOs. “The exit door is open, although it is not primarily opening through IPOs yet,” Piquet said. Taylor expects more exits could help bring global investors back consistently, with potential New York Stock Exchange listings by companies such as Wellhub , CloudWalk or Creditas contributing to another “rediscovery moment” in 2027. International investors remain interested in Latin America but have become more selective about deploying capital, according to Ana Cristina Gadala-Maria of QED Investors . Firms with a longstanding presence in the region remain engaged, while many that entered during the 2020–2021 investment boom have shifted toward AI opportunities elsewhere and are concentrating on existing portfolios, she noted. “Global investors are increasingly investing behind themes rather than geographies,” she said, putting Latin American startups in more direct competition with companies in the U.S. and other markets. Investor interest is increasingly centered on AI-native businesses and financial infrastructure, particularly stablecoins and cross-border payments. Gadala-Maria said more founders are targeting global markets from the outset, marking a departure from the previous wave of startups that adapted established business models to underserved local markets. “Increasingly, we’re seeing founders build globally competitive technology companies from Latin America, rather than necessarily for Latin America,” she said. Gadala-Maria agrees that Brazil and Mexico remain the region’s largest markets, with Brazil offering a deeper, more mature startup ecosystem and Mexico providing substantial room for financial services innovation. newContent: Crunchbase News https://news.crunchbase.com/ Data-driven reporting on private markets, startups, founders, and investors Mon, 19 Oct 2026 17:23:06 +0000 en-US hourly 1 https://wordpress.org/?v=6.8.11 https://news.crunchbase.com/wp-content/uploads/cb_news_favicon-150x150.png Crunchbase News https://news.crunchbase.com/ 32 32 How To Build A Billion-Dollar Company Without Venture Capital https://news.crunchbase.com/startups/bootstrapping-billion-dollar-company-ai-staffing-demarco-bairesdev/ Tue, 20 Oct 2026 11:00:46 +0000 https://news.crunchbase.com/?p=94248 By Nacho De Marco Today’s venture capital ecosystem looks markedly different from even just five years ago. Most significantly, a small number of AI companies are now attracting the vast majority of available venture capital. In Q1 2026, just four companies collectively raised $188 billion , which alone accounted for 65% of total global venture investment, per Crunchbase data. Meanwhile, in that same quarter, just 20% of global VC funding went to non-AI firms . Deal count was also down 30%, meaning that checks are being made out to fewer companies all around. So what happens to startups when the VC route is all but closed? I built a company into a multibillion-dollar business without any venture funding. Here’s a few lessons I picked up along the way: Prioritize customers and revenue, not fundraising Nacho De Marco, founding GP of BDev Ventures, and chairman of BairesDev. Many founders unknowingly treat fundraising as a measure of success. But while it’s useful, funding doesn’t result in success on its own. Achieving strong levels of customer trust is also helpful when it comes to inspiring investor confidence. High retention rates, repeat purchases and sustained engagement drive the financial fundamentals on which strong valuations are built. In B2B SaaS, for instance, companies with net revenue retention above 110% are valued at 2.4x the median . Additionally, customers provide a feedback loop that helps create the discipline every company needs, and each user is a vote of confidence that compounds over time. Going to market: Take time on pricing strategy Too many early-stage companies set prices too low because they fear that higher prices will repel customers. In my experience, however, underpricing more often signals uncertainty rather than good value. Customers want quality products and services, and they expect that the quality will be reflected in the price. Incredibly, only 22% of B2B SaaS firms conduct rigorous pricing research , and firms more commonly regret underpricing than overpricing. So at the outset, it’s important for startups to inform themselves what price their product or service can actually sustain, and then raise quality if it’s too low. Equally, in services markets where prices are more established around a norm, superior quality can be an important differentiator. At the same time, however, companies must continually resist the temptation to chase customers with ever-cheaper prices, which can start a race to the bottom. Hire the best talent Too many founders hire for speed rather than quality. Take the time needed to raise the bar with talent. Hire the right people, and they’ll help maximize every last drop of value. Many years ago, I decided to focus on just a small fraction of our applicants and hire only the top 1% of talent . When we found the best developers, it meant we could compete on delivery quality rather than just price. Keeping costs low is important, but skimping on talent is not a winning strategy. Use process automation efficiencies to drive growth One of our best decisions was to replace manual hiring processes with proprietary machine-learning systems at an early stage. Not only do these systems screen developer applications, but they can also build, match and deploy top-quality teams for each client project. This advance allowed us to cut costs associated with evaluating applications, accelerate lead times, and improve the quality of our teamwork. In parallel, we also invested in creating similar systems for our digital marketing so that growth wouldn’t require proportional increases in overhead. Whether it’s in recruitment, sales or operations, process automation can create some of the biggest drivers of growth and help bring about conditions needed for significant expansion to occur. Operate as if cash is running out tomorrow Companies thrive in challenging funding environments by operating with discipline. That means obsessing over unit economics, prioritizing activities that directly drive revenue, questioning every cost, and eliminating anything that isn’t pulling its weight. Not only does this aid growth, but it also makes a business more resilient in hard times. Financial constraints drive leaders to create efficiencies by automating workflows, streamlining processes and inventing innovative work models. Years before COVID-19 forced others to follow our lead, our company streamlined its operations and boosted scalability by developing a remote-working model. When the pandemic made remote work necessary, the fact that we already had the systems and workflows in place gave us a competitive advantage over other firms, and this in turn led to significant growth. Long term: Stay married to the problem, not the solution The past decade convinced many founders that venture capital was the default path to building a meaningful company. But while funding cycles rise and fall, the fundamental principles of good business don’t. Infusions of capital can accelerate growth, but they cannot create a great company from scratch. On the longest timescale, the most successful founders are the ones committed to solving problems rather than just selling a product and chasing funding. In a world short on funding, growth simply can’t happen without it. Nacho De Marco is the founding GP of BDev Ventures , and chairman of BairesDev , one of the largest bootstrapped nearshoring companies worldwide. Driven by his entrepreneurial spirit, he launched BDev Ventures in 2021 to help B2B companies accelerate their growth through a proprietary lead-generation platform. He also invests in and serves on the boards of biotechnology and e-learning companies. In recognition of his career path, he won distinctions such as an EY Entrepreneur Of The Year 2024 Bay Area Award. You will manage a team of Developer Advocates responsible for global programs such as Datadog Ambassadors, Champions, and User Groups, as well as opportunities for customer engineers to share their expertise through technical writing, public speaking, and other community contributions.<br><br><br>Across these interconnected programs, your team will enable customer engineers to contribute technical knowledge, lead communities, and turn their experiences into compelling content and conference talks for Datadog and third-party channels. This role combines people leadership, program strategy, technical judgment, and cross-functional influence to amplify authentic customer voices, deepen understanding of Datadog and its products, and foster a thriving community of practitioners.</p> <p>&nbsp;</p> <p><strong>What You’ll Do:&nbsp;</strong></p> <ul> <li>Lead and develop a team of Developer Advocates, setting clear expectations, guiding priorities, coaching performance, supporting career growth, and fostering an inclusive, high-performing culture</li> <li>Own the strategy, goals, and roadmap for Community Advocacy, translating broader Advocacy and company priorities into focused programs and measurable outcomes</li> <li>Guide the continued development of our Ambassador, Champion, and User Group programs, creating clear contributor journeys, expectations, enablement, recognition, and opportunities for customer engineers to increase their impact</li> <li>Build repeatable systems that enable customer engineers to contribute technical knowledge, create content, share best practices, and serve as trusted leaders within their communities</li> <li>Develop a strong pipeline of customer stories by identifying compelling practitioners and helping them shape authentic, technically credible narratives</li> <li>Oversee the support, co-development, and coaching of conference talks by customer engineers—from identifying an idea and developing an abstract through content review, rehearsal, and delivery—for Datadog events, including our flagship user conference, DASH, as well as third-party industry conferences</li> <li>Establish measures of success for Community Advocacy, using qualitative and quantitative insights to evaluate program health, contributor engagement, content quality, audience impact, and customer outcomes</li> <li>Partner closely with Product, Engineering, Marketing, Events, Customer Success, and regional teams to align priorities, identify opportunities, and scale customer participation across Datadog initiatives</li> <li>Ensure insights from Ambassadors, Champions, User Group participants, speakers, and other community members are shared with the appropriate teams inside Datadog, strengthening the connection between our customers and our products</li> <li>Balance strategic leadership with selective hands-on contribution, including coaching speakers, reviewing technical content, participating in community programs, and representing Datadog when appropriate</li> </ul> <p>&nbsp;</p> <p><strong>Who You Are:&nbsp;</strong></p> <ul> <li>You are an experienced people manager who has led autonomous technical professionals, coached performance, developed talent, and translated complex goals into achievable plans</li> <li>You have experience defining and delivering successful developer advocacy, developer relations, technical community, or a related functions</li> <li>You have built or meaningfully contributed to programs that enable external practitioners to participate, contribute, create content, or lead communities at scale</li> <li>You have experience helping technical practitioners develop and communicate their stories, including coaching conference speakers or co-developing technically credible talks and content</li> <li>You are a former software developer, SRE, or other technical practitioner—or have equivalent technical depth—with the judgment needed to assess technical accuracy and coach effective technical narratives</li> <li>You are a thoughtful cross-functional leader who can build alignment, make prioritization decisions, and influence partners across Product, Engineering, Marketing, Events, and customer-facing organizations</li> <li>You use both data and community insight to evaluate program effectiveness, identify opportunities, and make decisions about where the team should invest</li> <li>You understand how to build trust with technical communities and value authentic practitioner voices over purely promotional messaging</li> <li>You are comfortable operating through ambiguity, establishing structure where needed, and evolving programs as Datadog’s products, customers, and technical audiences grow</li> </ul> <p>&nbsp;</p> <p><em>Datadog values people from all walks of life. We understand not everyone will meet all the above qualifications on day one. That's okay. If you’re passionate about technology and want to grow your skills, we encourage you to apply.&nbsp;</em></p> <p>&nbsp;</p> <p><strong>Benefits and Growth:&nbsp;</strong></p> <ul> <li>New hire stock equity (RSUs) and employee stock purchase plan (ESPP)</li> <li>Continuous professional development, product training, and career pathing</li> <li>Intradepartmental mentor and buddy program for in-house networking</li> <li>An inclusive company culture, ability to join our Community Guilds (Datadog employee resource groups)</li> <li>Access to Inclusion Talks, our Internal panel discussions</li> <li>Free, global mental health benefits for employees and dependents age 6+</li> <li>Competitive global benefits</li> </ul> <p>&nbsp;</p> <p><em>Benefits and Growth listed above may vary based on the country of your employment and the nature of your employment with Datadog.</em></p> <p>#LI-Remote</p><div class="content-pay-transparency"><div class="pay-input"><div class="description"><p>Datadog offers a competitive salary and equity package, and may include variable compensation. oldContent: We Work Remotely: Remote jobs in design, programming, marketing and more https://weworkremotely.com/remote-jobs.rss We Work Remotely: Remote jobs in design, programming, marketing and more en-US 60 Datadog: Manager II, Developer Advocacy Anywhere in the World 🇺🇸 United States of America Product Full-Time <p> <strong>Headquarters:</strong> California, USA, Remote; New York, USA, Remote; Washington, USA, Remote </p> <p>Developer Advocates at Datadog are engineers who share their expertise with technical practitioners, help customers tell their stories, and represent the perspectives of our community inside Datadog.<br><br></p> <p>As a Manager II on the Advocacy team, you will lead our Community Advocacy functions. You will manage a team of Developer Advocates responsible for global programs such as Datadog Ambassadors, Champions, and User Groups, as well as opportunities for customer engineers to share their expertise through technical writing, public speaking, and other community contributions.<br><br><br>Across these interconnected programs, your team will enable customer engineers to contribute technical knowledge, lead communities, and turn their experiences into compelling content and conference talks for Datadog and third-party channels. This role combines people leadership, program strategy, technical judgment, and cross-functional influence to amplify authentic customer voices, deepen understanding of Datadog and its products, and foster a thriving community of practitioners.</p> <p>&nbsp;</p> <p><strong>What You’ll Do:&nbsp;</strong></p> <ul> <li>Lead and develop a team of Developer Advocates, setting clear expectations, guiding priorities, coaching performance, supporting career growth, and fostering an inclusive, high-performing culture</li> <li>Own the strategy, goals, and roadmap for Community Advocacy, translating broader Advocacy and company priorities into focused programs and measurable outcomes</li> <li>Guide the continued development of our Ambassador, Champion, and User Group programs, creating clear contributor journeys, expectations, enablement, recognition, and opportunities for customer engineers to increase their impact</li> <li>Build repeatable systems that enable customer engineers to contribute technical knowledge, create content, share best practices, and serve as trusted leaders within their communities</li> <li>Develop a strong pipeline of customer stories by identifying compelling practitioners and helping them shape authentic, technically credible narratives</li> <li>Oversee the support, co-development, and coaching of conference talks by customer engineers—from identifying an idea and developing an abstract through content review, rehearsal, and delivery—for Datadog events, including our flagship user conference, DASH, as well as third-party industry conferences</li> <li>Establish measures of success for Community Advocacy, using qualitative and quantitative insights to evaluate program health, contributor engagement, content quality, audience impact, and customer outcomes</li> <li>Partner closely with Product, Engineering, Marketing, Events, Customer Success, and regional teams to align priorities, identify opportunities, and scale customer participation across Datadog initiatives</li> <li>Ensure insights from Ambassadors, Champions, User Group participants, speakers, and other community members are shared with the appropriate teams inside Datadog, strengthening the connection between our customers and our products</li> <li>Balance strategic leadership with selective hands-on contribution, including coaching speakers, reviewing technical content, participating in community programs, and representing Datadog when appropriate</li> </ul> <p>&nbsp;</p> <p><strong>Who You Are:&nbsp;</strong></p> <ul> <li>You are an experienced people manager who has led autonomous technical professionals, coached performance, developed talent, and translated complex goals into achievable plans</li> <li>You have experience defining and delivering successful developer advocacy, developer relations, technical community, or a related functions</li> <li>You have built or meaningfully contributed to programs that enable external practitioners to participate, contribute, create content, or lead communities at scale</li> <li>You have experience helping technical practitioners develop and communicate their stories, including coaching conference speakers or co-developing technically credible talks and content</li> <li>You are a former software developer, SRE, or other technical practitioner—or have equivalent technical depth—with the judgment needed to assess technical accuracy and coach effective technical narratives</li> <li>You are a thoughtful cross-functional leader who can build alignment, make prioritization decisions, and influence partners across Product, Engineering, Marketing, Events, and customer-facing organizations</li> <li>You use both data and community insight to evaluate program effectiveness, identify opportunities, and make decisions about where the team should invest</li> <li>You understand how to build trust with technical communities and value authentic practitioner voices over purely promotional messaging</li> <li>You are comfortable operating through ambiguity, establishing structure where needed, and evolving programs as Datadog’s products, customers, and technical audiences grow</li> </ul> <p>&nbsp;</p> <p><em>Datadog values people from all walks of life. We understand not everyone will meet all the above qualifications on day one. That's okay. If you’re passionate about technology and want to grow your skills, we encourage you to apply.&nbsp;</em></p> <p>&nbsp;</p> <p><strong>Benefits and Growth:&nbsp;</strong></p> <ul> <li>New hire stock equity (RSUs) and employee stock purchase plan (ESPP)</li> <li>Continuous professional development, product training, and career pathing</li> <li>Intradepartmental mentor and buddy program for in-house networking</li> <li>An inclusive company culture, ability to join our Community Guilds (Datadog employee resource groups)</li> <li>Access to Inclusion Talks, our Internal panel discussions</li> <li>Free, global mental health benefits for employees and dependents age 6+</li> <li>Competitive global benefits</li> </ul> <p>&nbsp;</p> <p><em>Benefits and Growth listed above may vary based on the country of your employment and the nature of your employment with Datadog.</em></p> <p>#LI-Remote</p><div class="content-pay-transparency"><div class="pay-input"><div class="description"><p>Datadog offers a competitive salary and equity package, and may include variable compensation. Actual compensation is based on factors such as the candidate's skills, qualifications, and experience. In addition, Datadog offers a wide range of best in class, comprehensive and inclusive employee benefits for this role including healthcare, dental, parental planning, and mental health benefits, a 401(k) plan and match, paid time off, fitness reimbursements, and a discounted employee stock purchase plan.</p></div><div class="title">The reasonably estimated yearly salary for this role at Datadog is:</div><div class="pay-range"><span>$212,000</span><span class="divider">—</span><span>$265,000 US

The post Exa 3.0 Search API Tops Perplexity, Brave and Parallel on 8 Benchmarks appeared first on MarkTechPost . ]]> Exa has released Exa 3.0 , an upgrade to its web search API for AI agents. The Exa 3.0 search API ships a larger embedding model and a cheaper search type, Exa Lite. Dynamic Highlights is now generally available. Exa claims that it leads Perplexity, Brave and Parallel on 8 benchmarks. Those benchmarks were run by Exa, so you can treat them as self-reported. For developers, the practical change is cost: Lite costs $4 per 1,000 requests . TL;DR Size: Exa tracks over 2 trillion URLs and serves 100 billion pages. Embedding model size: Not disclosed. Runs on: Hosted API only. Exa lists configurable search latency of 450ms to 1s . No self-hosted option. Performance: Exa 3.0 Auto ranks first on all 8 Exa-run benchmarks against Perplexity, Brave and Parallel. Best: 91.8% on BrowseComp, plus the widest lead on ATLAS (42.0% vs 37.2% for Perplexity). Worst: 42.0% on ATLAS is its lowest percentage score. Its BrowseComp lead over Perplexity is only 0.3 points. What is Exa 3.0? Exa 3.0 is a search API release from Exa Labs that upgrades retrieval quality across every search type. It is available through the API. Exa runs its own crawler and an independent index. It is not a wrapper on Google or Bing results. How does Exa 3.0 improve retrieval? Exa attributes the gains to 3 changes in its retrieval stack: A larger embedding model : Exa trained it with more compute and data than any earlier model. Parameter count is not disclosed. Dynamic Highlights, now generally available : The model selects tokens across all results, not page by page. It gives more tokens to better pages and drops repeated information. Billions of new documents : New coverage includes products, local businesses, flights, events, sports and weather. According to the Exa’s post, Dynamic Highlights uses 95% fewer tokens than full page text while improving answer quality. Highlights carry no extra charge. That matters for agents, where context tokens often cost more than search calls. What is Exa Lite? Exa Lite is a new search type, set with type: "lite" on the /search endpoint, per the changelog . It runs on the same index as Exa Auto. Auto spends more compute on candidate generation, highlights and ranking. Lite supports query, result count, highlights, text, categories, domain and date filters, location and moderation. Unsupported parameters return a 400 error naming the field. Exa now recommends 3 search types: lite , auto and deep . The fast , instant and deep-reasoning types are legacy but still work. How does Exa 3.0 perform on benchmarks? Exa compared each provider’s highest-scoring single-step endpoint: Exa 3.0 Auto, Perplexity Web, Brave LLM Context and Parallel Advanced. All ran in one agentic harness. The agent was GPT-6 Luna, with up to 25 search rounds and 10 results per search. Evaluation happened in October 2026. The margins vary widely. ATLAS and WebCode show the clearest leads, at 4.8 and 5.6 points over Perplexity. BrowseComp, DSQA and WideSearch leads are each under 1.5 points over the runner-up. ATLAS is a benchmark Exa published itself on October 8, 2026. On cost, Exa plots agentic search score against cost per task. Lite scores about 79 at about $0.045 per task. Auto scores about 80.5 at about $0.065. Exa says the pair sets a new Pareto frontier among tested providers. How does Exa 3.0 compare with Perplexity, Brave and Parallel? No vendor has published matching results. Prices come from each vendor’s own pricing page. What data does the expanded index add? Exa states that it prioritized personal AI assistant use cases. The official technical page lists 1.27B ecommerce listings with prices and availability, and 211M+ local businesses . It also adds real-time news, sports, weather and market data, along with flights, events, transit and podcasts. The Exa Library structures this data into searchable collections. It runs eager by default, compiles through torch.compile and XLA, and replaces PyTorch/XLA for new workloads. The post Google Open-Sources TorchTPU, a Native PyTorch Backend for Cloud TPUs appeared first on MarkTechPost . ]]> Google has open-sourced TorchTPU , a native PyTorch backend for Cloud TPUs. It was co-developed with the PyTorch team at Meta and announced at PyTorch Conference 2026 on October 20, 2026. Existing PyTorch code targets a TPU through a standard torch.device("tpu") . TPUs now sit beside GPUs and CPUs as a native PyTorch device. Google team states that TorchTPU replaces PyTorch/XLA and recommends it for all new workloads. TL;DR Size: A software stack, not a model. 4 open repos: TorchTPU, vLLM-TorchTPU, SGLang-TorchTPU, TorchTitan. TorchTPU is v0.2.0 on PyPI , Python 3.11+, Apache 2.0. Runs on: Google Cloud TPUs. Tested on generations from v5e , scaled to 8,192 Ironwood (TPU7x) chips. Serving supports FP8, MXFP4 and NVFP4 checkpoints. Performance: Eager mode for debugging, torch.compile for production-level throughput. Best: 52% MFU training Qwen 3 8B with TorchTitan on Ironwood (self-reported). Worst: Out-of-box eager took 11.49s per step in a fine-tuning case, versus 2.78s fully tuned. What is TorchTPU? TorchTPU is an open-source PyTorch backend from Google and Meta that runs PyTorch models natively on TPUs. It plugs in through PyTorch’s PrivateUse1 interface . Tensors are ordinary PyTorch tensors, with no subclasses or wrappers. It runs one process per device and preserves tensor views and in-place mutations. The predecessor, PyTorch/XLA, recorded lazy-tensor graphs. Developers often added code to mark compilable regions. PyTorch/XLA also only supported pure SPMD code . TorchTPU also handles divergent MPMD execution. How does TorchTPU execute PyTorch code? TorchTPU ships 3 eager modes : Strict (default): dispatches each operator asynchronously with standard PyTorch semantics. Debug: runs synchronously with tensor bounds checking. DeferAndFuse: fuses runs of eager operators to cut HBM traffic. The TorchTPU paper says it can be 50% or more faster than Strict. For peak speed, torch.compile(backend="tpu") captures the graph with TorchDynamo. It lowers through StableHLO to OpenXLA, which emits TPU machine code. Compiled executables are cached across processes, hosts and job restarts. Custom Pallas kernels are callable as standard PyTorch functions. Prebuilt Tokamax kernels and Helion tile kernels also work. Distribution uses the tpu_dist process group. It supports DDP, FSDP2 and DTensor, along with a topology-aware mesh for TPU interconnects. How fast is TorchTPU? All figures below are self-reported by Google and partners. Training scale: TorchTitan reached up to 52% MFU on Qwen 3 8B . Google reports near-linear scaling up to 8,192 Ironwood TPUs. Tuning ladder: In a TorchTitan fine-tuning case, step time fell from 11.49s to 2.78s. DeferAndFuse alone gave 1.15x. Full torch.compile gave 3.80x . Model coverage: Google continuously tests about 5,000 Hugging Face models in eager and compiled modes. Fleet serving: Zenteiq grew daily output from 1.47B to 5.97B tokens per 1,000 TPU v6e chips. That gain came from llm-d routing on GKE, not TorchTPU alone. What integrations ship with TorchTPU? Hugging Face: Transformers v5 deploys to TPU with device_map="tpu" . Diffusers supports eager, torch.compile and tensor parallelism. vLLM-TorchTPU : built with Inferact. Keeps upstream schedulers and API servers, with custom Pallas kernels. SGLang-TorchTPU : built with RadixArk. Keeps RadixAttention prefix reuse. Serving features: FP8 KV caches, FP8, MXFP4 and NVFP4 checkpoints. Speculative decoding includes MTP and EAGLE-3. TorchTitan : recipes for Llama 3 70B/405B, Qwen 3 8B/32B, Qwen 3 235B MoE and FLUX.1 12B. Also: llm-d 1.0, Ray, TorchRec, VeRL (preview) and LiteRT-Torch for on-device export. How does TorchTPU compare with PyTorch/XLA, TorchNeuron and JAX? Feature TorchTPU ( repo ) PyTorch/XLA ( repo ) TorchNeuron ( AWS docs ) JAX on TPU ( Google docs ) Vendor Google + Meta Google / PyTorch AWS Google Hardware Cloud TPU (v5e and later tested) Cloud TPU Trainium 2, Trainium 3 Cloud TPU PyTorch device tpu xla neuron Not PyTorch Backend mechanism PrivateUse1 Lazy-tensor graph recording PrivateUse1 Not applicable Default execution Eager (Strict, Debug, DeferAndFuse) Lazy tensors Eager plus torch.compile Not disclosed Compile path TorchDynamo to StableHLO to XLA XLA Neuron Compiler XLA Distributed APIs DDP, FSDP2, DTensor, SPMD and MPMD Pure SPMD only FSDP, DTensor, DDP, TP Not disclosed Custom kernels Pallas, Tokamax, Helion Not disclosed NKI Pallas vLLM / SGLang serving vLLM-TorchTPU, SGLang-TorchTPU Not disclosed vLLM Neuron vLLM-JAX, SGLang-JAX Status Open source, v0.2.0 Being replaced by TorchTPU Public beta (Neuron 2.33) Maintained License Apache 2.0 Not disclosed Not disclosed Not disclosed How do you install TorchTPU? Install the package on a TPU VM, then pick the tpu device: Copy Code Copied Use a different Browser # pip install torch_tpu import torch device = torch.device("tpu") x = torch.randn((4, 4), device=device) The repo’s README pins torch_tpu==0.2.0 with the CPU PyTorch wheel index. Without it, pip pulls the CUDA build of torch . Full guides live at torchtpu.readthedocs.io . Key Takeaways TorchTPU is open source under Apache 2.0, co-built with Meta. It replaces PyTorch/XLA with eager-first, PrivateUse1-based execution. torch.compile(backend="tpu") lowers through StableHLO and XLA. TorchTitan hit 52% MFU on Qwen 3 8B, scaling to 8,192 Ironwood chips. vLLM, SGLang and Hugging Face now run on TPU through standard PyTorch. Check out the GitHub repo , paper , docs and Google Cloud announcement . All credit goes to the researcher of this project. You will help us build channels and funnels to bring the best engineering talent to our platform and match them with life-changing career opportunities.</p> <p><strong>Responsibilities</strong></p> <p>You have one job: grow the number of qualified and relevant candidates entering the platform.</p> <p>There is no second metric. Every day is spent moving that one number:</p> <ul> <li> <p>Iterate and scale channels that already work.</p> </li> <li> <p>Find and build new ones.</p> </li> <li> <p>Build the funnels and automation to make them scale without adding people.</p> </li> </ul> <p><strong>What we're looking for:</strong></p> <ul> <li> <p>A growth marketing background, with a proven track record of driving significant user and revenue growth.</p> </li> <li> <p>Experience across a wide variety of acquisition channels: inbound, outbound, communities, influencers, etc.</p> </li> <li> <p>Proficiency with analytics tools and a solid understanding of A/B testing methodologies.</p> </li> <li> <p>Demonstrated autonomy in driving growth initiatives.</p> </li> <li> <p>A “growth hacker” mindset, characterized by creativity, resourcefulness, and a relentless focus on improvement.</p> </li> </ul> <p><strong>To apply:</strong> <a href="https://weworkremotely.com/remote-jobs/lemon-io-growth-manager">https://weworkremotely.com/remote-jobs/lemon-io-growth-manager</a></p> Tue, 20 Oct 2026 13:23:25 +0000 Thu, 19 Nov 2026 13:23:25 +0000 https://weworkremotely.com/remote-jobs/lemon-io-growth-manager https://weworkremotely.com/remote-jobs/lemon-io-growth-manager Vertex Marketing Group: Distribution Engineer Anywhere in the World Lemesos Python, API, DevOps, Android, and iOS Back-End Programming Full-Time <img src="https://we-work-remotely.imgix.net/logos/0171/6611/logo.gif?ixlib=rails-4.0.0&w=50&h=50&dpr=2&fit=fill&auto=compress" /> <p> <strong>Headquarters:</strong> Bulgaria <br /><strong>URL:</strong> <a href="https://vertexmg.com">https://vertexmg.com</a> </p> <p><strong>Scale our distribution by code: a fleet of real devices, iPhones first and Android too, plus platform APIs and AI agents, posting across many accounts and surfaces. You work directly with the founder.</strong></p> <p>&nbsp;</p> <p>Most content gets made and then dies at a few hundred views, because getting it out is still done by hand: a person, a phone, a few accounts. We want it engineered: iPhone and Android device automation at scale, platform APIs and agents posting across many accounts and surfaces, every link tracked. If you would rather build that fleet than tap through posts one at a time, read on.</p> <p>&nbsp;</p> <p>Vertex Marketing Group builds AI creators and makes the content for real ones. Your job is to get that content out at a volume no team could post by hand, and keep the machine running. You own the outcome.</p> <p>&nbsp;</p> <p><strong>What you'll do</strong></p> <p>• Build and run the device fleet that posts by code: iPhones first, Android too, real devices and cloud phones</p> <p>• Publish across Instagram, TikTok, X, Reddit and Threads through platform APIs plus device and browser automation, hundreds of posts a day</p> <p>• Automate account health and posting cadence: every account checked every morning by code, problems caught before they cost reach</p> <p>• Put agents to work on the pipeline: Claude Code and MCPs handling captions, scheduling, health checks and recovery</p> <p>• Track every link: which account, post and surface sent each click, and what it turned into</p> <p>&nbsp;</p> <p><strong>Requirements</strong></p> <p>• You have built and run posting automation across 100+ accounts, and you can show it running</p> <p>• You have automated iPhones or other iOS devices (and/or Android, cloud phones) that run unattended</p> <p>• You work with platform APIs plus browser and mobile automation, with queues and scheduling</p> <p>• You run pipelines with Claude Code, MCPs and agents</p> <p>• Clear written English at minimum, perfect is better. Based in Europe or Latin America</p> <p>&nbsp;</p> <p><strong>Big plus:</strong> a development, infrastructure or DevOps background, and growth analytics: you read the numbers and know what to post more of.</p> <p>&nbsp;</p> <p><strong>Compensation</strong></p> <p>$4,000 to $6,000 per month, full-time, remote. Where you land in the range depends on what you show us. Same rate from day one of the paid test. Reviewed after 6 months.</p> <p>&nbsp;</p> <p><strong>Why Vertex?</strong></p> <p>• You own the outcome: your fleet, your numbers, your call on what goes out where</p> <p>• You work directly with the founder, in a small team of sharp people who are fun to work with</p> <p>• Content to distribute every day, and the budget for the devices and the stack</p> <p>• The mission: become one of the best in the world at this, fast, then package what we build for other agencies</p> <p>• Fast decisions. You'll know within 48 hours at every stage</p> <p><strong>To apply:</strong> <a href="https://weworkremotely.com/remote-jobs/vertex-marketing-group-distribution-engineer">https://weworkremotely.com/remote-jobs/vertex-marketing-group-distribution-engineer</a></p> Tue, 20 Oct 2026 11:32:37 +0000 Thu, 19 Nov 2026 11:32:37 +0000 https://weworkremotely.com/remote-jobs/vertex-marketing-group-distribution-engineer https://weworkremotely.com/remote-jobs/vertex-marketing-group-distribution-engineer Datadog: Manager II, Developer Advocacy Anywhere in the World 🇺🇸 United States of America Product Full-Time <p> <strong>Headquarters:</strong> California, USA, Remote; New York, USA, Remote; Washington, USA, Remote </p> <p>Developer Advocates at Datadog are engineers who share their expertise with technical practitioners, help customers tell their stories, and represent the perspectives of our community inside Datadog.<br><br></p> <p>As a Manager II on the Advocacy team, you will lead our Community Advocacy functions.
